Poor ventilation systems in modern office buildings are recycling old, stale air and spreading airborne infections. Various studies have found instances where tuberculosis, measles, and flu were spread throughout sealed, modern office buildings that added little or no fresh air. Other places where infections spread rapidly include airplanes, pediatricians' offices, prisons, hospitals, and homeless shelters. Adding 15, or even less than 10, cubic feet per minute of outdoor air has become common. Adding even 35 cubic feet per minute as recommended in Massachusetts would significantly decrease infection's spread, but can be expensive.

Poor ventilation in modern office buildings is causing spread of flu and other airborne infections including measles and tuberculosis, according to public health experts. One office building reported an outbreak of TB among 40% of workers, traced to one sick employee. Many modern buildings are sealed to conserve energy, recirculating indoor air. Airborne infections may be carried throughout buildings, infecting workers far from the source. The amount of outdoor air in such buildings needs to be increased. Airplanes, waiting rooms, homeless shelters, prisons and hospitals are likely sites for spreading infections.

Unlike many conventional systems for making loans in the world, making a microloan to a Third World small business entrepreneur is almost a guarantee of repayment. Recipients want the security of a favorable credit rating. These microloans cancel out the need to get involved with loan sharks. Third world banks and large development organizations are making such loans as well, particularly when they discovered that the repayment rate by the poor is nearly 100 percent. Some charitable organizations still prefer to make per-to-person sponsorships and the teaching of skills to improve the quality of life.

U.S. development organizations are finding that some of the world's poorest entrepreneurs repay their debts at rates approaching 100%. Their repayment performance shines when compared with that of many sovereign nations. Tiny Third World businesses commonly repay "microloans" faithfully because they crave the security of a favorable credit rating. The money helps them start or expand their businesses "selling vegetables, sewing, repairing shoes, making furniture and the like" and boosts their local economies. Through microlending U.S. development groups believe they are exporting free-market economics to tiny businesses that can fuel growth in the developing world.

Micro-enterprise lending is now booming. U.S. development groups believe this support to grassroots enterprises is a way to export free-market economics and fuel growth in the developing world. One group, Accion, plans to increase micro-lending in Latin America to $66.5 million this year and expand to between $500 million and $1 billion by 1996. Other participants include CARE of New York, Trickle Up, and Save the Children. Some Third World banks are paying attention. Individual loans are between $50 and $500, while repayment rates continue to be above 90%. The U.S. Agency for International Development has doubled its micro-enterprise budget from 1988.

While some Democrats claim term limits are a "right-wing" crusade, this author (John Fund) believes support from the liberal and Democratic sphere is increasing. Polls show Americans back term limits by 75% to 21% nationwide. One reason is that term limits would open up politics to people--minorities and women--now excluded from office. Some past Democratic leaders were cited as supporting the idea, but the party "apparatchiks" remain against it. Some journalists favor term limits voicing a need for new blood and the end of professional politicians. Fund does not believe enacting term limits will be easy.

House Speaker Tom Foley spoke out against term limits in Washington state, asserting that the proposal is supported by right-wing activists. Ron Brown, Democratic Chairman, says the idea is an attempt by Republicans to get rid of those that can't be beaten at the polls, but a CBS poll shows Americans overwhelmingly favor the limits with very little demographic variation. Term limits, it is believed, will open up politics to blacks and women, among other minorities. Democratic party officials are dead set against the proposal and threaten those that support it with blacklisting. Many governors, other state officials and well known journalists support limits.

Are term limits a crusade driven by only one party or ideology? Many believe the movement is GOP sponsored in order to oust incumbent Democrats. However, it is now picking up many prominent liberal and Democratic supporters. One reason is that it would help many people such as blacks, other minorities and women, now excluded from office by incumbents. Democratic Party leadership still opposes term limits, believing they would result in large GOP gains. But, as a sign of the times, term-limit opponents are now relying more on judges to stop the movement than on trying to convince voters to reject the idea.
